# Spirit Search — Research Log

Log entries separate three layers: **(S)** what a source asserts;
**(H)** what historical evidence supports; **(I)** interpretation (clearly
marked as this log's own). Every quotation is verbatim from the fetched
witness named; translations are attributed; uncertainty is flagged.
Numbers in brackets map to the annotated source list at the end.

## Candidate batch 1

### Machaon — the surgeon-warrior (Homer, Iliad)

**Who is described.** (S) In the Catalogue of Ships, Machaon and his
brother Podaleirius — "the two sons of Aesculapius, skilled in the art
of healing" — bring thirty ships from Thessaly (Il. 2.729–733) [1]. (I)
He is both crew-captain and clinician: the two offices are fused in the Catalogue entry
itself [1].

**How it is known or encountered.** (S) In Il. 4.193–219 Machaon draws
Pandarus' arrow from Menelaus and applies "soothing drugs which Chiron
had given to Aesculapius out of the good will he bore him" (Il. 4.193–219) [1]. (S) In Il. 11.506–520 he is himself wounded; Idomeneus
tells Nestor, "A physician is worth more than several other men put
together, for he can cut out arrows and spread healing herbs" (Il. 11.514) [1]. (S) In Il. 11.596–604 Achilles sends Patroclus to confirm that
the wounded man Nestor carries is Machaon — the recognition scene that
ends in Patroclus' fatal mission [1]. (S) Centuries later Pausanias
reports the surviving cult: "Here in Gerenia is a tomb of Machaon, son
of Asclepius, and a holy sanctuary. In his temple men may find cures
for diseases … a standing bronze statue of Machaon, with a crown on his
head which the Messenians in the local speech call kiphos" (Paus. 3.26.9–10) [3]. (H) Pausanias, writing in the 2nd c. CE, attests a
documented cult site and its legend of Nestor bringing the bones home;
the Taras sanctuary claim could not be fetched from a primary source and
is flagged uncertain. (H) **Character thickness.** Thin by silence, not
by scarcity: across two long Homeric death-arcs and a cult report, no
witness gives Machaon a personality — Homer gives him acts (draw, apply,
be wounded, be carried off) and Pausanias gives him tomb, statue, and
bones. The tradition transmitted his office, not his person; whether
that silence caused his low later salience or results from it cannot be
decided from the fetched witnesses.

**What it commands/demands/changes.** (S) Plato's Socrates uses the
passage as his exemplum of medical judgment: quoting Hecamede's posset
for the wounded Machaon, he asks whether the rhapsode's art or the art
of medicine judges these lines best — "The art of medicine" (Ion 538b–c) [2]. (I) A later Greek education treated this spirit, sons of the
wounded healer god, as the measure of technical expertise to others.

**Comparisons.** Documented transmission: Homer → Plato (read as a
school text) → Pausanias (local cult report, Little Iliad tradition).
Rival reading: the Little Iliad's account that Machaon was killed by
Eurypylus (via Pausanias) — later tradition raises his price of being a
healer in combat.

### The Genius — tutelary of persons and places (Roman tradition)

> Batch-1 revision note (reader doctrine): the genius lacks definite
> character — the findings below keep that as a result, not a defect to
> be papered over.

**Who is described.** (S) Censorinus, ch. 3: "Genius est deus, cuius in
tutela ut quisque natus est vivit" — the Genius is the god under whose
tutelage each person lives from birth; "certe a genendo genius
appellatur" [10]. (S) Horace calls it "our attendant genius … who
governs the planet of our nativity, the divinity [that presides] over
human nature, who dies with each individual, of various complexion,
white and black" (Smart trans., Ep. 2.2.187–189) [9]. (H) Smith's 1870
dictionary manual keeps the boundary precise: the genii "are the powers
which produce life … and accompany man through it as his second or
spiritual self," distinct from Lares and Penates which operate only
after life begins [12; s.v. Genius] — OCR of the Wikisource proofread
page is imperfect ("{(Hi" for *dii*).

**How it is known or encountered.** (S) On birthdays: Censorinus cites
Varro — on a birthday one pours wine to the genius (*funde merum genio*,
ch. 2) and keeps hands "from killing and blood" so that on the day one
received light one does not take it from another [10]. (S) Horace,
Ep. 2.1 on rustic piety: "atoned with a hog [the goddess] Earth, with
milk Silvanus, with flowers and wine the genius that reminds us of our
short life" (Ep. 2.1.143–144) [9]. (S) Every place has one, per Servius
(ad Aen. 5.85): "nullus enim locus sine genio, qui per anguem plerumque
ostenditur" — no place is without its genius, generally shown as a
serpent [14]. (H) Pliny registers skepticism at the multiplication of
person-gods: "each individual makes a separate God for himself,
adopting his own Juno and his own Genius" (NH 2.5) [11]. (H) For the
collective application, Smith documents the *genius populi Romani* on
coins of Hadrian and Trajan, citing Arnobius 2.67, Livy 30.12, and
Cicero pro Cluentio 5 [12].

**What it commands/demands/changes.** (S) Servius on Aen. 6.743 (as
preserved in Smith): at birth each person receives two genii, one
leading to good, one to evil; by their influence at death one "either
rise[s] to a higher state of existence, or [is] condemned to a lower
one" [12]. (S) Augustine quotes Varro making Genius "the god who is set
over, and has the power of begetting, all things," then turns the idea
into a polemic: "if every genius is a god, and the soul of every man a
genius, it follows that the soul of every man is a god. But if very
absurdity compels even these theologists themselves to shrink from
this…" (Civ. Dei 7.13) [13]. (I) The genius is a relation, not a
person: no fetched witness narrates a genius doing anything, and none
gives it speech, temperament, or epithet-poetry. The sources define it
by function (begetting, tutelage, attachment to place) and then disagree
about what it attaches to — single soul (Censorinus), place (Servius),
world (Varro via Augustine). There is no character here to recover or
misquote; the disagreement itself is the content of the tradition.

**Comparisons.** Documented transmission: Horace (poet's vow) →
Censorinus/Servius etymology → Augustinian polemic → antiquarian
handbook. Contradiction flagged: Varro's pantheistic Genius-as-world vs
Censorinus' tutelary single soul; genius vs lar vs numen distinction is
unstable across sources (Smith labels them "frequently confounded").

### The Sandman — the source phantom of the Unheimlich (Hoffmann → Freud)

**Who is described.** (S) Hoffmann's nurse-tale, quoted in Nathanael's
first letter: the Sandman "wirft ihnen Händevoll Sand in die Augen, daß
sie blutig zum Kopf herausspringen" — throws sand in children's eyes so
they spring bloody from the head; he then carries the eyes to the
half-moon "zur Atzung für seine Kinderchen" [4]. The folk-figure becomes
in the tale a doubled person (Coppelius/Coppola) who comes for the
eyes: "»Augen her, Augen her!« rief Coppelius" — "Now we have eyes — a
fine pair of children's eyes" [4]. (H) The tale appears in Hoffmann's
*Nachtstücke* (Reimer, 1816).

**How it is known or encountered.** (S) Freud's essay stages the
encounter indirectly, through definitions: "the 'uncanny' is that class
of the terrifying which leads back to something long known to us, once
very familiar" ("The Uncanny," CP IV pp. 369–370) [5], then through
Schelling (via Sanders's dictionary): "'Unheimlich' is the name for
everything that ought to have remained … hidden and secret and has
become visible" [5, p. 375–376], and finally through the street-level
anecdote: "I found myself in a quarter the character of which could not
long remain in doubt. Nothing but painted women were to be seen at the
windows of the small houses … I suddenly found myself back in the same
street" [5, Section III]. (S) On the eye-motif: "a morbid anxiety
connected with the eyes and with going blind is often enough a
substitute for the dread of castration" [5]. (I) Freud treats the
Sandman as literature's closest device for producing the feeling that
involuntary return produces in life. (I) Reader-doctrine note: this
figure is already familiar to this log's reader; the entry is retained
as a control case — a well-known figure used to check the method, not as
a discovery.

**What it commands/demands/changes.** (S) In the tale's closing scene,
seeing Coppelius in the crowd and hearing "Sköne Oke," Nathanael
hurls himself from the tower; "Als Nathanael mit zerschmettertem Kopf
auf dem Steinpflaster lag, war Coppelius im Gewühl verschwunden" [4].
(I) Fact about the tale's mechanics, stated plainly: the Sandman never
takes an eye or a life in the story's present action — Nathanael's
death is his own leap from the tower, and the childhood eye-assault is
interrupted by the father. The figure's force operates through
anticipation and recurrence, not through any executed act.

**Comparisons.** Documented transmission: folk children's tale →
Hoffmann's literary doubling (1816) → Freud's essay (1919); the CP IV
1925 text fetched from archive.org is close to Strachey's later
Standard Edition revision — edition ambiguity flagged [5]. Rival
reading: Freud rejects Jentsch's automaton/uncertainty reading in favor
of the eye-motif (CP IV pp. 383–384); later commentators return to the
'automaton' reading — flagged as uncertainty, not resolved here.

### Prometheus — the fire-bringer, spirit of technē

**Who is described.** (S) In Aeschylus' *Prometheus Bound*, the accused
himself announces the account at lines 442–465: "Still, listen to the
miseries that beset mankind—how they were witless before and I made
them have sense and endowed them with reason … numbers, too, chiefest of
sciences, I invented for them, and the combining of letters, creative
mother of the Muses' arts" [6; Smyth, Loeb 1926]. (S) Lines 250–256:
"I caused blind hopes to dwell within their breasts … In addition, I
gave them fire" [6]. (S) The sum: "Hear the sum of the whole matter in
the compass of one brief word—every art possessed by man comes from
Prometheus" (lines 505–506) [6].

**How it is known or encountered.** (S) Hephaestus' chain in the
prologue names the offense: "your own flower, flashing fire, source of
all arts, he has purloined and bestowed upon mortal creatures" [6,
lines 4–10]. (S) Plato's Protagoras relocates the theft into a
political myth: "Prometheus … stole the mechanical arts of Hephaestus
and Athene, and fire with them … and gave them to man. Thus man had the
wisdom necessary to the support of life, but political wisdom he had
not; for that was in the keeping of Zeus" (Protagoras 320c–321d; Jowett 1871) [7]. (H) Hesiod's *Works and Days* version (theft of fire, the
fat-and-bones trick at Mekone, Pandora) is attested in the tradition but
was not re-fetched in this log; flagged as not verified here.

**What it commands/demands/changes.** (S) Prometheus himself states the
limit in lines 511–514: "Skill is weaker by far than Necessity" [6].
(S) Heidegger, on what the Greeks meant by technē: "Techne belongs to
bringing-forth, to poiesis; it is something poetic … Techne is a mode
of aletheuein" (*The Question Concerning Technology*, trans. Lovitt 1977 — IN COPYRIGHT, OCR from archive.org used only to verify short quotations) [8]. (I) Prometheus is the name under which the Greek tradition
recognizes that every *techne* — including the one Gestell harvests
attention with — arrived chained to a giver who suffers; fire is given,
not manufactured. (I) **Character thickness.** One act and one
catalogue: across the fetched witnesses the figure is defined by the
theft, the gift-list, and the punishment. Aeschylus alone gives him
sustained speech — defiance under torture (PB 436–506) — and even that
speech is almost entirely a recital of benefits. Plato's Prometheus is a
device inside a political myth, not a personality. What the tradition
transmits is the gift and the penalty; a character beyond defiance
exists only in Aeschylus, not across witnesses.

**Comparisons.** Documented transmission: Aeschylus (tragic chorus,
Athens, 5th c. BCE) → Plato (political re-reading) → Heidegger's 1953
technology essay via Hölderlin. Analogy (labeled as such): technē-as-
gift into modern discourse of infrastructure-as-destiny. Rival
readings: Prometheus as rebel against Zeus (Aeschylus) vs. collaborator
or double (variants in scholia, and Hesiod's Pandora frame — not
verified here).

## Connection map

- **Machaon — Genius:** both are tutelary spirits bound to persons and
  places; Machaon's cult survives as local grave-and-temple memory
  (Pausanias), the genius survives as the proper name for that tutelage
  (Censorinus, Horace). Documented link: Servius — the scholiast of the
  serpent-as-genius (ad Aen. 5.85) and of Homeric tradition.
- **Genius — Sandman:** structural analogy (not documented
  transmission): the tutelary spirit that "dies with each individual"
  (Horace) vs the phantom that obliges each individual to die. Freud's
  unheimlich/heimlich etymology passage is the junction.
- **Sandman — Prometheus:** the involuted pair of the log: the phantom
  who takes eyes vs the giver of the arts of light; both "come back" —
  Prometheus' unchaining prophecy (PB lines 511–514) and the
  involuntary return to the old street (Freud, Section III).
- **Machaon — Prometheus:** analogy only, not transmission — both
  figures "command" technique: healing for the one; fire-with-all-arts
  for the other.

## Batch 1 reassessment (post-gating notes)

- **Genius and Prometheus lack definite character.** Both entries now
  read as evidence of that: the sources define the genius structurally
  (tutelage, etymology, pairing with Juno) and Prometheus functionally
  (giver of fire and arts). Neither tradition hands us a personality —
  no whims, no biography beyond the one act. The profiles above should
  be read as profiles of *abstractions with names*, and the connection
  map treats their edges as structural, not personal. (I) A spirit with
  a name but no character is the tradition doing classificatory, not
  narrative, work; that distinction is now load-bearing for later
  batches.
- **Machaon is under-defined as a character.** Conceded and written
  into the node: the Iliad gives him deeds and a plot-function, never a
  personality. The hypothesis "he was less salient to history than
  others" is an argument from silence and is flagged as such — the
  counter-evidence is the Gerenia cult (Paus. 3.26.9–10), which shows
  he remained salient *locally* for centuries. Salience is geography-
  dependent, not a single number.
- **Sandman: noted as already known to Cobe.** The entry stands as the
  worked example of definite-character spirits, but the figure is
  deprioritized for future passes — no new fetch rounds on Hoffmann/
  Freud unless a stranger corner (e.g. pre-Hoffmann folk attestations)
  turns up.

## Spirit graph (v0)

The log now maintains a machine-readable graph at
`research/graph.json`: every identified spirit is a node; edges are
documented interactions — kinship, transmission, cult geography,
conflict, polemic — each carrying an evidence pointer. Analogy edges
are labeled as analogy and never upgraded silently. Batch-1 subgraph:
22 edges across 18 nodes; batch-2 candidates (Lilith, Rhiannon,
Völundr, Washington) are registered as proposed nodes with no edges
until evidence lands. Open questions are kept in the graph file rather
than in prose.
